Article Title: Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
Article Text:
Delhi CM Rekha Gupta poses for a group picture during an on-site inspection of waste disposal operations near Okhla, in New Delhi

Government targets legacy and fresh waste

New processing plants at three sites

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What is your top concern regarding pollution in Delhi? Landfill waste Air quality Water quality (Yamuna) Dust pollution 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Focus on pollution and waste management

NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.
Article Summary: Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years. She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure.

Article Title: India-US trade talks hit ‘plateau’: Sitharaman says further give-and-take ‘very, very difficult’
Article Text:
Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman

India stresses strategic autonomy in trade negotiations

India-EU pact opens market access

India and US have reached a “plateau” in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement, with further concessions from either side likely to be "very very difficult", finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, she said that while negotiations are still underway, any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side.“The agreement negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” Sitharaman said.She said the agreement was still being “hard and very rigorously negotiated” and that India has a trade surplus with the US. “But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favor.”Sitharaman said that the US would naturally want to reduce this trade imbalance and address what it sees as losses built up over the years.She also said that the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.“Negotiation used to be the only platform through which countries could highlight the discrepancies, highlight the lop-sidedness and say, would we want to correct this?” she said.“Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it. Today framework is there, tariffs are going,” she said, while stressing that countries still need to negotiate and find “some give and take”.Sitharaman was also asked about maintaining strategic autonomy while negotiating bilateral trade agreements with European countries, including in the context of India procuring Russian oil."There is no Lindsay Graham Bill in Europe...," she said.On the broader question of how bilateral trade agreements can protect a country's interests in an era of multilateralism, Sitharaman said countries were increasingly choosing bilateral partnerships where they saw greater benefit.“Countries choose where multilateralism would benefit them, and there are some unique bilaterals which countries choose to have. The balance is somewhat tilted in favour of the bilateral rather than the multilateral,” she said.She said countries were now increasingly looking for new trade partners and strengthening those relationships through agreements.“Countries are now rapidly catching up with — I would put the EU-India also in a bilateral mode -because it's one in the name of union, but of course within them they have. So, bilaterals today are catching up far more than even initiating or beginning a multilateral. It's not deliberate, but in a way, if you don't do it, you're not moving forward. Countries will have to choose new partners for their trade and strengthen the tie through an agreement. And therefore, newer partnerships are being searched for, and they are tied up bilaterally.”FM Sitharaman cited the India-EU trade agreement as a major example of India's approach to negotiating trade pacts while protecting domestic interests.She said India had opened 92.5 per cent of its tariff lines and around 97 per cent of tariff value under the agreement. The EU, meanwhile, had opened 99 per cent in value terms and possibly 97 per cent of tariff lines.According to Sitharaman, greater access to the European market could support employment in labour-intensive sectors, including footwear, textiles, toys and processed products. Many of these sectors are linked to micro and small enterprises.“Those are all in the micro and small medium industry segment, which are labor-intensive,” Sitharaman said, adding that greater access to the European market could generate “more exports, more jobs”.Sitharaman said bilateral trade agreements were becoming increasingly important as multilateral institutions have weakened.“Multilateralism is not going to go away. But multilateralism has weakened,” she said.She also stressed that multilateralism should continue even as countries increasingly pursue bilateral agreements.“Multilateralism is not going to go away and multilateralism shouldn't go away,” Sitharaman said.The Munich Leaders Meeting, being held in the National Capital, provides a platform for about 100 senior decision-makers and experts to discuss opportunities for stronger cooperation among emerging and middle powers amid profound geopolitical change. Discussions include geoeconomic developments, trade and connectivity, maritime security, defence cooperation and other key international challenges.
Article Summary: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman says India and US have reached a 'plateau' in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement. She said any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side. She also said the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.

Article Title: LPG consumption down, diesel & petrol sales up in September
Article Text:
LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier

NEW DELHI: LPG demand fell by over 9% year-on-year in Sept, while petrol and diesel sales registered growth of 7% and 5%, respectively, provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) showed.LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier.Month-on-month consumption, however, registered a growth of 8%, up from 2.4 MT.Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT. Petrol and diesel consumption had registered year-on-year growth of 7.9% and 6.5%, respectively, in July.While petrol is largely used as an automobile fuel and its consumption is commensurate with the increasing number of vehicles, diesel is consumed by transport vehicles for passenger and freight movement, besides being used in the agricultural sector.Erratic monsoon conditions due to El Nino boosted demand for diesel for irrigation.Cumulative petrol consumption during Apr-Sept in the current financial year increased 7% to 22.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose 4.8% to 47.9 MT. In contrast, LPG consumption declined 14.9% to 13.8 MT from 16.2 MT during the corresponding period of 2025-26.
Article Summary: LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier. Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT.

Article Title: In 2012, Taylor Swift pledged $4 million for a Nashville education centre; 14 years later, the space is showcasing artwork by local schoolchildren and artists with developmental disabilities
Article Text:
Taylor Swift

A major gift for education

Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ mansion: Inside the $47 million Beverly Hills home where her music video was filmed(Image Credit: Instagram)

Learning by making

Two groups, one exhibition

A centre still doing its job

​In 2012, Taylor Swift donated $4 million to Nashville’s country music museum; 14 years later, its education centre gives local artists a platform(Image Credit: Instagram)

From a pledge to a public platform

Connection

Taylor Swift’s $4 million gift to the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum in 2012 helped create a dedicated education centre in Nashville. The space was designed for more than music lessons: it would give children and families room to learn, experiment and engage with country music’s history. Fourteen years later, the centre is hosting Connection, an exhibition of posters created by Metro Nashville Public Schools students and artists from Friends Life Community, a nonprofit serving adults with developmental disabilities. The museum says the participants explored the history and techniques of Hatch Show Print, its historic letterpress shop, before making their own work. The exhibition brings the centre’s original educational promise to life, showing how a space built for learning can keep opening doors to creativity and community.In May 2012, Swift pledged $4 million towards a new education centre at the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum. According to MusicRow, it was the largest capital contribution by an individual artist in the museum’s 45-year history at the time. The museum named the centre in her honour.The gift formed part of a wider expansion campaign called 'Working on a Building: Country Music Lives Here'. The museum planned to grow from 140,000 square feet to more than 350,000 square feet, creating additional exhibition and learning spaces as well as new visitor facilities.The Taylor Swift Education Center was planned as a space of more than 7,500 square feet, spread across parts of two floors. Its design included three classrooms and a children’s exhibition gallery. The museum expected its new facilities to increase its educational capacity by as much as sevenfold.The planned classrooms were intended for a range of activities, from the museum’s flagship Words & Music programme to family events and distance learning. One “wet classroom” was designed for hands-on projects that could get messy, including letterpress art activities connected to Hatch Show Print.The centre’s original vision was not limited to traditional classroom instruction. The museum planned spaces where students could explore objects, observe curators at work and take part in activities that made music history tangible. A visible storage area and design studio would allow visitors to see how museum professionals handle and interpret collections.That hands-on approach is reflected in the centre’s current exhibition, Connection. Opened in 2026, the show brings together posters made by Metro Nashville Public Schools students and artists engaged with Friends Life Community. The project began with visits to Hatch Show Print, the museum’s nearly 150-year-old letterpress shop. Students learned about the shop’s history, studied design principles and explored how letterpress printing works. They then created shapes using foam and sponges, printed those forms and used them as inspiration for their finished posters, as per reports.The process gave participants a chance to learn not only by looking at art, but by making it. They experimented with words, images, colour and composition, using the print shop’s techniques to develop their own visual ideas.The exhibition also grew from a collaboration between the museum and Friends Life Community, which serves adults with developmental disabilities. Friends Life invited Hatch Show Print Master Printer Emeritus Jim Sherraden to work as a teaching artist in residence in 2023. In late 2024, artists from Friends Life Community visited the print shop for a behind-the-presses tour. Sherraden and Jennifer Haston, the organisation’s visual arts programme coordinator, helped participants bring their words, lettering and images to life through poster-making, as per reports.The posters created by both groups form the exhibition’s central focus. The museum says the works use action words and imagery to imagine a future where people connect through creative art and social causes. The title Connection speaks to the ideas behind the exhibition, but also to the relationships built through the process: between students and artists, participants and printers, and the public and the museum.The project demonstrates how a museum education space can bring people together across ages and abilities. It also gives visitors the opportunity to encounter work made by members of their own community, rather than only by established artists or historical figures.When Swift made her pledge, the museum described the centre as a place for school groups, families, young people and adults. The new exhibition shows how that original ambition continues to shape the space more than a decade later.The education centre is not simply a room named after a famous musician. It is part of the museum’s broader effort to connect people with country music and its creative traditions through participation. In Connection, that means learning about letterpress printing, trying the process and producing posters that reflect the creators’ own ideas.The exhibition is open to museum visitors, with admission included in the price of a museum ticket. The museum also offers free admission for local youth and discounted tickets for up to two accompanying adults from Davidson County and neighbouring counties, with proof of residency.Swift’s generous contribution of $4 million played a crucial role in creating a lasting educational component within one of Nashville’s most iconic cultural institutions. The carefully designed classrooms, a dedicated children’s gallery, and interactive programming were all put in place with the intention of transforming the museum into more than just a location for viewing exhibitions. These elements were strategically crafted to provide visitors with opportunities to learn through hands-on experiences and active participation.Fourteen years later, the original idea has taken shape through, an exhibition featuring colourful posters created by local students and artists with developmental disabilities. Working together, they explored a traditional printing technique and used it to share their personal experiences, ideas and perspectives.However, it is important to note that this exhibition does not represent the conclusion of the center's evolving narrative. Instead, it serves to illustrate the extraordinary outcomes that can arise when a cultural institution commits resources and efforts toward creating a dedicated physical space, fostering educational opportunities, and promoting creative accessibility over an extended timeframe. A generous gift made in 2012 laid a solid foundation for establishing this creative setting; now, the individuals who engage with it today are actively populating that environment with their own creative works, innovative ideas, and meaningful connections.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments section below.
Article Summary: Taylor Swift donated $4 million to the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum in 2012. The centre was designed for more than music lessons: it would give children and families room to learn, experiment and engage with country music’s history. Fourteen years later, the centre is hosting Connection, an exhibition of posters created by Metro Nashville Public Schools students and artists.

Article Title: In 2005, two Ohio brothers bought a flooded quarry for $330,000 and spent 15 years improving it; 21 years later, the village abandoned its bid to seize the 72.5-acre site and now has a $206,000 judgme
Article Text:
After learning about the proposed sale, the Village of Luckey began considering acquiring the property itself. (AI photo)

15 years of improving quarry

What happened at the auction?

Court rejected brothers' claims

Village abandons acquisition but faces bill

What legal bill mean for Luckey

Two brothers in Ohio who bought an abandoned, flooded quarry for $330,000 in 2005 and spent 15 years improving it have been caught in a long legal dispute with the village where the property is located. Steve and Tim Snyder had planned to sell the land in 2021, but the Village of Luckey began proceedings to acquire it through eminent domain, a legal power that allows governments to take private property for public use with compensation.The dispute continued for nearly five years before the village abandoned its attempt to acquire the property in April this year. However, the legal battle has left Luckey facing approximately $206,000 in legal fees, with a judgment lien now recorded against the village.According to a report by The Blade, the amount represents nearly one-third of the village's general fund balance of approximately $640,000 at the end of 2025. The payment has not yet been made because the property owners are challenging the settlement agreement reached by their former lawyer.The case began with a failed property auction in September 2021. The brothers alleged that village officials had discouraged potential buyers from bidding, while Luckey maintained that it wanted the quarry as a possible public water source.The disagreement eventually reached the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, where the brothers' federal constitutional claims were dismissed.Steve and Tim Snyder purchased the inactive quarry and surrounding land in March 2005 through their company, T&S Agriventures LLC. They paid $330,000 for the property, intending to improve it for future development or sale.Over the following 15 years, they worked on the land's topography and grading, cleared vegetation, established electricity and sanitary sewer services, and maintained the quarry lake. Their aim was to make the property suitable for residential or other development.In July 2021, the brothers hired Beth Rose Real Estate and Auctions LLC to market the property. An auction was scheduled for September 18, with a reserve price to prevent the land from selling below an agreed amount.However, after learning about the proposed sale, the Village of Luckey began considering acquiring the property itself. In August 2021, the village council unanimously authorised its attorney to begin the eminent domain process. Officials initially identified a public water supply or park as possible uses, before later specifying water supply alone.Days before the auction, village officials told the brothers that any purchase offer would depend on laboratory results assessing the quarry's water. They also indicated that the eminent domain process could take several years.On the auction day, the village placed temporary 'No parking; signs on nearby public streets. Its representatives attended the event but did not bid.The brothers alleged that the officials' presence discouraged buyers. After bidding closed at $610,000, the property remained unsold because the highest offer was below the reserve price.According to the court documents, the auction company later contacted registered bidders, several of whom said the village's actions had influenced their decision not to bid.The village continued pursuing the land and, in September 2022, offered the brothers $525,000. The dispute subsequently moved into court.The Snyders and their auctioneer filed a federal lawsuit alleging violations of constitutional protections concerning private property, equal treatment and due process.In February 2024, a federal district court dismissed their claims. The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals subsequently upheld that decision.The majority ruled that the village's announcement of its intention to acquire the property did not itself amount to an unconstitutional taking. It noted that the brothers still owned the land and that the $610,000 auction bid demonstrated the property had not lost all economic value.However, Circuit Judge Eric Clay disagreed in a dissenting opinion. He argued that the brothers had presented sufficient allegations of deliberate interference with the auction to allow their takings claim to proceed.The majority also acknowledged concerns about aspects of the village's conduct but concluded that the allegations did not establish a constitutional violation.Luckey continued its attempt to acquire the quarry until April 2026, when the village council formally abandoned the eminent domain proceedings.The decision led to a settlement involving legal fees, with a $206,000 judgment lien recorded against the village in the Wood County Court of Common Pleas.However, the settlement remains disputed. Steve Snyder alleged in court documents that the family's former attorney, Zachary Murry, agreed to the settlement in July without consulting them.The family is seeking to reverse the agreement because it prevents further claims against individual village officials and limits recovery to legal fees rather than additional damages.The village's payment was due on August 15, but Mayor Mike McNulty said officials were waiting for the court to resolve the dispute over the settlement.Luckey, a village of approximately 1,000 residents, ended 2025 with $640,217 in its general fund, according to financial statements cited by The Blade. Its annual revenue was approximately $1.16 million.The potential legal payment is therefore a substantial expense for the village. Nevertheless, McNulty maintained that essential services, including streets, sewer operations and other everyday functions, were not at risk."The village is able to operate functionally," he told The Blade. "We're not going to be able to go and build a swimming pool or something like that. The everyday function of the village, streets, sewer, things like that- the village is fine."What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments section below.
Article Summary: Steve and Tim Snyder bought an abandoned, flooded quarry for $330,000 in 2005 and spent 15 years improving it. They planned to sell the land in 2021, but the Village of Luckey began proceedings to acquire it through eminent domain. The dispute continued for nearly five years before the village abandoned its attempt to acquire the property in April this year. However, the legal battle has left Luckey facing approximately $206,00 in legal fees.

Article Title: In 2022, Ryan Reynolds and Blake Lively gave $500,000 to Water First; four years later, the Canadian charity's latest graduating class included eight newly certified Indigenous water operators
Article Text:
(Instagram)

A donation aimed at local training

Eight new operators graduate

Why local operators matter

A continuing water challenge

Building skills for the long term

In 2022, Ryan Reynolds and Blake Lively donated $500,000 to Water First, a Canadian charity that works with Indigenous communities on water education and training. Four years later, the organisation marked a milestone: eight Indigenous trainees had graduated from a 15-month programme as certified water operators. The graduates completed more than 2,000 hours of hands-on training and passed the exams required for certification, according to Water First. Their achievement points to the long-term purpose of the 2022 gift, which was intended to help more Indigenous young adults train for water-related careers. The donation did not solve Canada’s drinking-water challenges on its own, but it supported a locally focused approach: building skills so communities can strengthen their own capacity to manage water systems.When Reynolds and Lively announced their donation in March 2022, they said it would support Water First’s education and training programmes for Indigenous youth and young adults. The funds were intended to help train water treatment plant operators and environmental water science technicians, as well as introduce school-aged students to water science. Reynolds described access to clean drinking water as a basic human right and said the couple valued Water First’s focus on training Indigenous adults to become certified operators and technicians.Their contribution supported a charity that works alongside communities to develop programmes shaped by local priorities, rather than relying on a single, identical solution for every place, as per the report.Water First says its partnerships are built around collaboration with Indigenous communities. Local leaders help identify needs and shape the training, with the goal of developing expertise within the communities themselves. That approach recognises that the challenges facing one water system may differ from those affecting another.The need for trained local operators is one part of a wider picture. Communities can face issues involving infrastructure, water quality or a shortage of people qualified to operate treatment systems. Training does not replace necessary equipment or investment, but it can help communities build the people and knowledge needed to manage water systems over the long term.Eight participants graduated from a Drinking Water Internship programme in May 2026, organised through a partnership between Water First, the Anishinaabeg of Kabapikotawangag Resource Council, participating communities and Big Island First Nation. The 15-month programme included classroom lessons and practical training, with each participant completing more than 2,000 hours of hands-on experience. They also took four exams required to obtain Water Operator certification. The training prepared them to operate and maintain drinking-water treatment systems and pursue careers in water treatment and related environmental fields. The skills they gained can also help their communities manage local water facilities.One graduate, Brandon Penner of Big Grassy First Nation, said the programme pushed him beyond his comfort zone and helped him recognise what he could achieve through commitment. He also spoke of a deep connection to the natural world and a desire to protect it for future generations.For many communities, having trained local people involved in water management can make a difference to both daily operations and long-term self-sufficiency. Water First’s announcement quoted Rhonda Nash, director of operations at AKRC, saying that certified operators were needed for the council’s five member First Nations, which include seven separate communities, two of them remote. Nash said the goal was to ensure access to clean drinking water while creating employment and enabling community members to operate their own treatment plants. The model links technical training with local jobs and community capacity.That work is important because water systems require skilled people to monitor processes, respond to problems and maintain consistent operations. The graduates’ certification gives them a professional foundation, while their local knowledge and relationships can help connect technical work with community needs.Water First says its internship alumni can also access continuing career development and education through an expanding professional network. That support matters because training is not a one-time event. Operators may need ongoing learning as their responsibilities grow and water-management challenges change.The graduation comes amid persistent drinking-water concerns in Indigenous communities across Canada. Water First’s May 2026 release said 16% of First Nations were affected by a drinking-water advisory, with the figure rising to 32% in Ontario. The charity cautioned that the issue is complex, involving different combinations of infrastructure, source-water quality and staffing needs.Those figures help explain why the organisation focuses on partnerships and locally designed programmes. No single intervention can address every cause of unsafe or unreliable water. Communities may need infrastructure improvements, source-water protection, technical expertise and sustained funding, often at the same time.Water First frames training as one part of the solution, not a substitute for broader action. Developing local expertise can help communities operate systems and strengthen their ability to respond to challenges, while wider infrastructure and policy needs remain.The eight new operators are part of a growing network. Water First reported that 73 interns from 47 Indigenous communities had graduated from its internship programmes to date, logging approximately 170,000 hours working in local water plants and attending workshops.Those numbers represent more than training hours. They reflect the development of experience that can remain within communities and support future generations. A certified operator can help a community manage a water system today, while also becoming a mentor or resource for others pursuing similar work.Reynolds and Lively’s $500,000 donation helped Water First expand its capacity to offer hands-on training to more Indigenous youth and adults. Four years later, the graduation of eight operators shows one concrete outcome of that broader effort. The donation was one contribution among many, alongside funding from government programmes, community partnerships and other supporters.The water challenges facing Indigenous communities are far from resolved. But the new graduates represent an important step towards local capacity, skilled employment and stronger community involvement in water management. Their certification gives them tools to protect a resource that communities depend on every day, and helps keep the work of building a more sustainable future close to home. Their progress also shows how sustained training and community partnerships can help turn support into lasting change.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments section below.
Article Summary: Eight Indigenous trainees have graduated from a 15-month programme as certified water operators. The graduates completed more than 2,000 hours of hands-on training and passed the exams required for certification. Their achievement points to the long-term purpose of the 2022 gift, which was intended to help more Indigenous young adults train for water-related careers.

Article Title: Oil prices climb as Houthis step up attacks on Saudi Arabia, stoking supply fears
Article Text:
Oil prices rise to to $106.58 a barrel (AI-generated image)

Oil prices rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the risk of supply disruptions from escalating attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia against expectations of increased Russian diesel exports easing market tightness.Brent crude futures rose 89 cents, or 0.8%, to $106.58 a barrel by 0030 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 80 cents, or 0.9%, to $94.94. Article Title: Amid AI push, no internet in 48% of Karnataka schools
Article Text:
Karnataka is introducing AI skills in schools, with significant challenges in internet accessibility (AI image)





BENGALURU: While Karnataka is favouring introduction of AI skills and coding in its schools, nearly 48% of the state’s 74,578 schools do not have internet connectivity, exposing a glaring digital divide.According to UDISE+ report released by Union ministry of education for 2025–26, the state’s connectivity rate is well below the national average of 67%. Nearly one in three schools in India lacks internet access, while every second school in Karnataka lacks the facility.Home to the country’s IT capital, Karnataka has the highest percentage of schools without internet connectivity among the southern states — both as a proportion of total schools and in absolute numbers.The gap is particularly alarming in government schools. Of the state’s 48,527 government-managed schools, only 18,007 have internet facilities, leaving about 30,520 (63%) without connectivity.These contrasting figures come at a time when chief minister DK Shivakumar, during his Independence Day, announced the AI Akshara Abhiyana and Coding Gurukula initiatives across Karnataka, aimed at introducing AI education in schools from Class 6.Subsequently, the CM said AI training had already begun for Class 9 students in govt schools and directed officials to explore extending it to younger students, with support from the information technology department and private organisations. However, the widening infrastructure gap raises questions about how uniformly these initiatives can be implemented across the state.D Shashi Kumar, general secretary of the Associated Managements of Primary and Secondary Schools in Karnataka (KAMS), pointed out that the digital divide could widen if the number of schools with functional internet connections were considered, as several schools reporting internet access do not have an active connection.“AI education requires access to computers, suitable software, trained teachers and, for many learning applications, reliable internet connectivity. Without these basic facilities, students in poorly connected schools risk being left behind even as their peers gain exposure to emerging technologies. Although the government has pinned its hopes on CSR initiatives, how many schools will these initiatives cover? All these programmes require substantial financial resources. Will the government be able to provide the necessary funds?” he asked.Karnataka’s performance is also poor compared with that of its southern neighbours. Andhra Pradesh has internet access in 99.2% of its 60,843 schools, while Tamil Nadu has achieved 99% coverage across 57,566 schools. Kerala reports connectivity in 92.6% of its 15,750 schools. Telangana, despite having a sizeable gap of its own, has internet access in 76.5% of its 41,762 schools. Karnataka, with connectivity in just 51.7% of its schools, has the lowest coverage in South India, the report revealed.“The proportion of schools without internet connectivity in Karnataka is more than twice that of Telangana, where 23.5% of schools lack access, and over six times the national average of 32.6%,” a Bengaluru-based academician said.Nationally, 4.77 lakh of India’s 14.67 lakh schools lack internet access, according to the report. Karnataka accounts for approximately 7.5% of the nationwide deficit.
Article Summary: Nearly 48% of the state’s 74,578 schools do not have internet connectivity, exposing a glaring digital divide. Nearly one in three schools in India lacks internet access, while every second school in Karnataka lacks the facility. Karnataka has the highest percentage of schools without internet connectivity among the southern states.

Article Title: MDR on UPI transactions over Rs 2,000 deferred; to come into effect post Diwali
Article Text:
Govt defers 0.4% merchant discount rate on UPI payments

MUMBAI: Its official. There will be no MDR on UPI until the festival season is over. The National Payment’s Corporation of India’s The UPI and Services Steering Committee has deferred the implementation of merchant discount rates (MDR) on select person-to-merchant UPI transactions until immediately after Diwali, citing the festive season. The implementation date will be notified separately.The Times of India had reported last week that finance ministry and the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) have decided to defer the introduction of merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions, seeking to avoid adding to business costs and hitting consumption at a time of economic headwinds, people aware of the matter said. The revised rollout was expected to be pushed to January 2027 from October 15. However,the announcement on Tuesday states that the implementation will be immediately after Diwali.The MDR framework was approved and notified by NPCI on September 15, with a 0.4% charge for eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above. The framework was to take effect from October 15, giving banks, payment aggregators and other ecosystem participants a month to make operational changes.Also read: Pakistan angle under probe? Delhi Police files 4 FIRs over fake posts since Oct 10 The decision to defer the rollout comes just days before the scheduled start and follows demands from trade bodies and merchant associations for a January implementation. They have argued that introducing the fee during the festive season, when retail activity and digital payments typically rise, could increase costs for merchants and weigh on sales.The framework was designed to create a revenue stream for the payments ecosystem after more than six years of effectively zero MDR on UPI. The government had said the levy would apply only to specified merchant transactions, with payments up to Rs 2,000 and eligible small merchants continuing to remain free. About 96% of P2M transactions were expected to remain unaffected.The deferment gives merchants and payment companies more time to prepare while allowing the government to avoid introducing a new transaction cost at a potentially sensitive point for consumption.
Article Summary: There will be no MDR on UPI until the festival season is over. The revised rollout was expected to be pushed to January 2027 from October 15. The announcement on Tuesday states that the implementation will be immediately after Diwali. The MDR framework was approved and notified by NPCI on September 15.

Stock market rally

today:

posts sharp gains

Comments by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax and securities transaction tax, along with a rally in IT stocks and other factors, lifted investor sentiment.BSE Sensex ended the day at 73,033.78, up 1,109 points or 1.54%. Article Title: BFI feud deepens: Secretary General Pramod Kumar alleges intimidation as Rs 40 crore boxing deal takes centre stage
Article Text:
Representational image (Credit: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The battle for control of the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) intensified on Tuesday, with secretary general Pramod Kumar alleging intimidation of state associations and attempts to derail a proposed no-confidence motion against president Ajay Singh , even as the federation featured in a major Rs 40 crore partnership aimed at strengthening Indian boxing.In letters to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, union sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya and World Boxing (WB) president Gennadiy Golovkin, Kumar sought intervention to protect affiliated state units from alleged threats of suspension and the appointment of ad-hoc committees. Copies of the letters are with TOI.Kumar alleged a breakdown in governance and accused Singh and BFI executive director Col (retd) Arun Malik of using administrative machinery to obstruct the process for moving the no-confidence motion. He claimed that a majority of state units and executive committee members had submitted requisitions seeking a vote on Singh's leadership.The motion is scheduled to be taken up at a special general meeting on Oct 28. Kumar maintained that, as secretary general, he was duty-bound to act on the requisitions and uphold the federation's constitution. He also alleged that his official email access had been revoked without his consent, hampering his work and raising concerns about the security of federation records.Kumar further claimed that state associations backing the motion were facing pressure and threats, and expressed concerns for his personal safety. He urged the authorities to ensure that the federation's records were safeguarded and that the alleged administrative interference stopped.Malik, however, dismissed the allegations as “baseless”. “All these allegations are baseless and not true. We have done no such thing," Malik told PTI.Malik also denied that Kumar’s email access had been revoked. “Nobody has revoked his email access. He can get it checked, we have no issues," he told the newswire agency.The governance row unfolded against the backdrop of a significant push for boxing development, with the National Sports Development Fund (NSDF), Sports Authority of India (SAI) and Indian Oil Corporation signing a memorandum of understanding to support the sport.Under the agreement, Indian Oil will contribute Rs 40 crore over two years towards talent identification, athlete development, coaching, sports science, international exposure, boxing academies and capacity-building for coaches, referees and technical officials.Mandaviya said corporate social responsibility-backed partnerships would play a key role in building a national sports ecosystem, in line with the revamped Khelo India scheme. The MoU signing was attended by senior sports ministry and SAI officials, where Singh and Malik were also present. Singh later interacted with the minister as well.The partnership comes after Indian boxers won six medals, including three gold and three bronze, at the 2026 Asian Games, underlining the need to strengthen the pathway from grassroots talent identification to elite competition.With the Oct 28 vote approaching, the BFI faces a crucial test on two fronts: sustaining investment in the sport while resolving an increasingly bitter internal dispute over its leadership and governance.
Article Summary: Boxing Federation of India (BFI) secretary general Pramod Kumar alleges intimidation of state associations. Kumar seeks intervention to protect affiliated state units from alleged threats of suspension and appointment of ad- hoc committees. BFI president Ajay Singh and BFI executive director Col (retd) Arun Malik accused of using administrative machinery to obstruct the process for moving the no-confidence motion.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says AI has made coding faster, but it has not yet …
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

Sridhar Vembu: AI is increasing costs for software companies

“a) server/memory and hardware prices are way up (4-5x in a year for servers) driven by the monster AI data center build out.

b) AI token spending per engineer is way up (those productivity gains are costly!)

c) Hosting open weight models needs expensive GPUs.”

“Layered on top of that is the geopolitical uncertainty. As one example, the Middle East is a major market and the prolonged war is not good. The US stock market is in a monster bubble and it is a mistake to think of stock prices as indicative of future prosperity - the GFC of 2008-9, dotcom bust of 2001-2 as wall as the 1980s Japan bubble all demonstrate that point,” Vembu added.

Sridhar Vembu: 10x productivity leap in software is coming

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu said that AI is making software development faster, but it has not yet made the process 10 or 100 times more productive. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), Vembu said that such a leap could happen in the future, putting pressure on software jobs. “As of today, AI led productivity gain in software development estimates are (at best) 25% to 50% as measured on an end to end product basis (prototyping is much much faster now but finished product requires a lot more human work),” he said in the post adding “A 10x or 100x productivity leap could happen (I believe it will happen, see below) but it has not happened _yet_”.In the post, Sridhar Vembu also pointed to three major expenses that companies are incurring because of AI. These include:Vembu says that the 10x productivity leap in software is coming “because of what is happening in the mathematics world. The crucial link is auto-formalization, or formal verification of code. Mathematics theorems are formalized in Lean and proofs are verified by the Lean verifier - Lean is a programming language”.“LLMs do not verify the proof, they generate it to be verified by the Lean verifier and once you have the advanced reasoning capable LLM and Lean verifier in a feedback loop and give plenty of compute, magic happens,” he said.He also shared an analogy explaining how formal automated verification mechanism is coming to LLM generated software. “The analogy is handloom weaving vs powerful machine looms of code,” he wrote.Concluding the post, Vembu wrote “So it is the combination of current data center/AI costs, geopolitical uncertainty and the potential of a 10x or bigger leap in software productivity driven by advances in automatic program verification. These are all challenges to software jobs, and that is why we have called for reinvention internally”.
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu said that AI is making software development faster, but it has not yet made the process 10 or 100 times more productive. He said that such a leap could happen in the future, putting pressure on software jobs. He pointed to three major expenses that companies are incurring because of AI.

Article Title: How hackers taking control of hundreds of refrigerators in supermarkets across France may have 'proved' Europe's fears of China deactivating hundreds of its buses right on the roads 'true'
Article Text:
The French refrigerator attack

Echoing Europe’s nightmare over Chinese connected buses

A cyberattack that hijacked commercial refrigeration units across hundreds of French supermarkets has offered a real-world demonstration of the dangers lurking in connected infrastructure. For European officials, the incident does more than spotlight digital vulnerabilities in the food supply – it provides a warning and fuel to growing anxieties across the region that internet-linked transit systems, including hundreds of public buses built by Chinese manufacturers, could be remotely immobilised right on the roads during a crisis.The Paris prosecutor’s office launched an investigation this week following an overnight cyberattack targeting cooling systems across multiple French grocery chains. Attackers breached central management panels, overriding controls to force refrigeration and freezer units into non-stop defrost cycles at 50°C (122°F). This resulted in fires, melted equipment and dumpsters full of spoiled food, with French retail group Les Mousquetaires (operator of Intermarché and Netto) reporting losses reaching millions of euros.France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) confirmed the attack targeted Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series controllers.Danfoss acknowledged the breach, stating the affected units ran “outdated firmware” and noting that it “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions.”The supermarket breach underscores a core vulnerability: once a piece of infrastructure is connected online for diagnostics, anyone with system-level access – whether a malicious hacker or the manufacturer itself – can override its physical operations.That exact mechanism was at the heart of the panic in Scandinavia, where transport operators in Denmark and Norway, last year, started probing Chinese-built electric buses over fears they could be remotely weaponized or shut down.Scrutiny centered on Yutong, the Zhengzhou-based company that ranks as the world’s largest bus maker by sales volume. Danish transport operator Movia, which runs 262 Yutong buses across Copenhagen and eastern Denmark, warned that over-the-air (OTA) functionality creates severe exposure.“Because these buses can receive updates and diagnostic tests 'over the air,' they can be stopped remotely, either by the manufacturer or by a hacker,” Movia COO Jeppe Gaard told NBC News.Norwegian transit agency Ruter, which oversees half of Norway’s public transport, conducted controlled tests “inside a mountain” comparing Yutong vehicles against Dutch-made VDL models. While Dutch buses lacked automated OTA functions, Yutong maintained “direct digital access to each individual bus,” leading Ruter to conclude that the fleet could, in theory, be rendered completely inoperable by the manufacturer.In response, Yutong stressed that it “strictly complies with the applicable laws, regulations, and industry standards,” noting that its European Union operational data is encrypted and housed in an Amazon Web Services facility in Frankfurt, Germany.
Article Summary: Attackers hijacked commercial refrigeration units across hundreds of French supermarkets. French retail group Les Mousquetaires ( operator of Intermarché and Netto) reported losses reaching millions of euros. The supermarket breach underscores a core vulnerability: once a piece of infrastructure is connected online for diagnostics, anyone with system-level access can override its physical operations.

Article Title: Texas rejected a settlement that would have cut a proposed data center from 2,523 acres to 1,375; commissioners also denied the developer’s permit appeal as a court fight now looms
Article Text:
AI image for representation purpose

Why commissioners rejected the settlement

Developer says court action is likely

Why are residents opposing the project

Texas' Hood County commissioners have rejected a settlement that would have reduced a proposed data center project from about 2,523 acres to 1,375 acres. They also unanimously denied the developer's appeal against an earlier decision to reject permits for the project, bringing a possible court fight closer. The decisions came on Tuesday, October 13, after hours of public testimony and debate over the Comanche Circle data center project. Developer Sailfish Investors had reportedly offered to reduce the project's size and make commitments on water-efficient cooling, building setbacks, light pollution and road repairs in an effort to reach an agreement with the county.However, commissioners voted 3-1 against the settlement, with Kevin Andrews the only member voting against its rejection. Commissioner Nanette Samuelson was absent. The commissioners later voted unanimously to deny the developer's permit appeal.The proposed Comanche Circle campus, led by Sailfish managing partner Ryan Hughes, is planned near the Hood and Somervell county line, close to Dinosaur Valley State Park. Residents raised concerns about the project's possible effects on water supplies, wildlife, nearby properties and local roads.Questions were also raised about drainage, power generation and the project's water source. Opponents argued that the developer had not provided enough information and proper plans.Kevin Andrews said the county should continue discussions with the developer rather than reject the settlement.“We have been offered concessions that we can’t regulate, and I think it would be a good idea for us to continue to negotiate to try to get to terms that work for the county,” Andrews said.The proposed settlement included closed-loop cooling, which is designed to reuse cooling water, along with light pollution controls and other commitments. Hughes also said he would not seek tax incentives if the agreement was approved. However, commissioners rejected the deal and then voted against the appeal of the earlier permit decision.In an October 1 email to county officials, Ryan Hughes warned that rejecting the settlement could lead to a lawsuit and potentially leave the project subject to fewer restrictions. Before the vote, he told commissioners, “It looks like we’re unfortunately going to court.”After the decisions, Hughes said he was disappointed but not surprised. In a statement sent to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, he said he had agreed to reduce the project's size and include water-efficient cooling and light pollution controls.“When Governor Abbott set his commonsense data center standards, I agreed with them wholeheartedly and committed Comanche Circle to them,” Hughes wrote.He added: “I hoped today’s settlement would end this dispute for good. Instead, neighbors lose those protections and taxpayers pay for a court fight the County could have avoided,” he said.Hughes also apologised during the meeting for using profanity in text messages discussed by speakers at the hearing.“That’s how I talk to my friends. That’s how I talk to colleagues. And you know, it’s something that my wife says I really hope to work on. So I definitely apologize for the language and apologize for any insinuations,” he said.Residents and local groups, including Protect the Paluxy Valley, have opposed the proposed campus over concerns about its impact on water resources and the surrounding environment. Commissioner Dave Eagle said Hood County has a special designation under state law, known as Subchapter 231K, which covers the watershed that drains into Lake Granbury and the Brazos River.Eagle said the law gives the county powers intended to protect public health and safety and prevent pollution of rivers and lakes. Texas counties are still working out how to regulate large data centre projects while balancing the interests of developers, property owners and local communities.With the settlement rejected and the permit appeal denied, Sailfish Investors faces another setback in its effort to move forward with Comanche Circle. The company had argued that the settlement would allow the project to proceed with additional restrictions, but commissioners chose not to approve the agreement.
Article Summary: Texas' Hood County commissioners rejected a settlement that would have reduced a proposed data center project from about 2,523 acres to 1,375 acres. They also unanimously denied the developer's appeal against an earlier decision to reject permits for the project. Developer Sailfish Investors had reportedly offered to reduce the project's size and make commitments on water-efficient cooling, building setbacks and light pollution.

Article Title: Michael Dell joins debate on 'safeguards and controls' for AI models; sends 'strong message' to government, OpenAI and Anthropic
Article Text:
AI is not wiping humanity

Sees no AI bubble

Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell warned that artificial intelligence requires strict safeguards and controls, weighing in on an escalating national debate over the existential risks posed by rapidly advancing AI systems. Speaking on CNBC, Dell framed the emergence of artificial intelligence through the lens of foundational human technologies. “I think we’ve always had technology that can do great things and maybe do some not-so-great things,” Dell said. “You know, fire can heat your home. It can also burn down your whole village. So that’s not good. So we have to have safeguards and controls.”Dell emphasized that both the public and private sectors bear responsibility for managing these risks. While calling on AI developers to establish "bounded permissions" within their tools, he acknowledged that government intervention is necessary. However, Dell declined to outline specific legislative or policy measures, noting that he is not a policymaker.Dell also doesn't believe that AI is coming to kill humans.
